files.text:
Nelumbo nucifera

The Leaf that Stays Dry

Rain on the sacred lotus, which never wets it.

Rain does not wet a lotus leaf. A drop lands, springs up a little, and comes to rest as a bead so round that it seems to sit on the leaf rather than touch it, and at the slightest tilt it rolls away like mercury spilled on a table. Under a microscope the reason is plain. The upper side of the leaf is crowded with papillae, domes of living cells ten or twenty thousandths of a millimetre high, and every one is furred with tubules of wax far finer still. The drop rests on their tips, on a cushion of trapped air, and touches perhaps a fiftieth of the surface beneath it. It meets the leaf at an angle of about a hundred and sixty degrees, very nearly a whole sphere, and a tilt of a few degrees is enough to set it going.

It rolls, rather than slides, and that is the point. Whatever lies in its path, a speck of soot, a grain of pollen, the spore of a mould, holds to water more readily than to wax, and is taken up on the surface of the drop and turned over and over as it travels, and carried off. In 1997 the botanists Wilhelm Barthlott and Christoph Neinhuis, asking why some leaves always come out of the rain clean, called this the lotus effect, and it has since been copied into paint, glass and cloth. The plant had it first. It roots in the mud of still ponds, and its leaves stand clear of the water all summer, unmarked.

Small beads stop where they land, held by a vein or a hollow. Larger ones run, and meet, and become one with a shiver, and anything bigger than a few millimetres across is pressed flat by its own weight. The leaf is a shallow cup, and the water finds its way to the middle, over the place where the stalk joins beneath, and gathers into a single pool that shines like quicksilver. Under it, between the water and the leaf, there is still a film of air, and it is that film you see, holding the light. Tip the leaf and the pool goes out over the edge in a rush, onto the leaf below or into the pond with a small ring, and the leaf is as dry as before.

press a leaf, or push a beadtip the phone, or press a leaf

# lotus-leaf Rain on a cluster of lotus leaves. Five to seven real leaves, cut out along their own rims, lie on the paper as if on still water: some float flat, others stand above them on stalks, one large leaf dominant, one high leaf tipped and seen half on edge, the higher ones larger and casting soft warm shadows on the leaves below and on the paper. A single closed pink bud stands among them, the one touch of colour, its stalk hidden under the big leaf. When the pond comes into view a shower passes over it. On every leaf the drops come to rest as beads so round they hardly seem to touch it, and they shine like quicksilver: the tiniest are points of silver, the bigger ones little lenses with a silver margin, and in each leaf's cup they gather into one flat, sky-bright pool. Drops that miss the leaves make faint grey rings on the paper, as on water. Tip the phone, press and hold a leaf, or push a bead with a finger or the mouse, and the beads roll on every leaf at once, merge with a quick shiver, pick up the dust in their path, and run off the edge: onto the leaf below, or down to the water with a ring. A stalked leaf nods when a heavy drop lands on it, and settles. Tip everything clear and after a moment another light shower comes. The leaves start grey-green and their colour deepens as the rain lands. ```html ``` Each `` is a cut-out leaf (alpha = the leaf; same origin, since WebGL and the physics read it). `data-navel` is where the stalk joins under it and `data-radius` its mean radius, as fractions of the image. The figure sets its own aspect ratio (1.18 wide, 0.86 on a narrow column, below 560 px) and the script lays the leaves out from the two images, varied by rotation, mirroring, size and a slight shift of hue. Or call `lotusLeaf(figure, options)` yourself; it returns `destroy()`, which also has `.state()`, `.rain(n, radiusMM)` and `.tip(x, y)` (-1..1, as if the phone were tipped) for tests and tinkering. A third `` (optional) is the bud: drawn among the leaves, no physics, its colour arriving a little ahead of the leaves'. Without JS or WebGL the two leaves lie on the paper as a still group. ## Options On the figure (`data-*`) or in the options object, which wins. | attribute | option | default | | |---|---|---|---| | `data-water` | `water` | `none` | `none`: the leaves lie on the paper, their shadows and the rings on it in faint warm greys. `wash`: a broad, very pale wash of water under the cluster, fading over 40-80 px with no outline | | `data-span` | `span` | `420` | the pond's width in mm on a wide layout (300 on a narrow one). Sets the scale: leaves are 55-150 mm across, beads 0.3-2.8 mm in radius | | `data-shower` | `shower` | auto | drops in the shower when the pond first comes into view (about ten seconds). Auto is one per 95 mm² of leaf, 120-1000: 40% fine (0.3-0.7 mm, they stay where they fall), the rest small, medium and big; big ones throw off a few tiny satellite droplets | | `data-rain` | `rain` | `9000` | ms between the sparse drops after the shower (jittered ±40%); `0` = none | | `data-drops` | `drops` | `14` | how many sparse drops before the sky clears | | `data-seed` | `seed` | `7` | the leaves' relief, the dust, the pond's outline and where the rain falls | The layouts (`LAYOUT_WIDE`, `LAYOUT_TALL` at the top of the script) give each leaf its place, size, height above the water (0 = floating), image, rotation, mirroring, hue and, for a stalked leaf, how far it is tipped and which way. ## Events All bubble from the figure, with `detail: { r }` (the drop's radius in mm): | event | when | |---|---| | `lotus-leaf:land` | a drop strikes a leaf (from the sky or from a leaf above) | | `lotus-leaf:merge` | two beads touch and become one (beads under 0.45 mm stay quiet) | | `lotus-leaf:runoff` | a bead goes over a leaf's edge | | `lotus-leaf:splash` | a drop reaches the water (and makes a ring) | ## Theming | variable | default | | |---|---|---| | `--accent` | clay | keyboard focus ring | The pond's colour (`water` in the script) is a pale grey-green, the sky it mirrors. The leaves' grade is in the shader (`grade()`, `SAT0`/`SAT1`): the photographs' blue-green with a faint waxy bloom, from 24% saturation when dry to 74% once wet. ## The real thing - **The lotus effect** (Barthlott and Neinhuis, 1997): papillae 10-20 µm high covered in wax tubules trap air; water meets the leaf at about 160° with tiny contact-angle hysteresis, so drops *roll* at a tilt of a few degrees. Modelled as a rolling bead (a share of g·sinα, with viscous loss) held by hysteresis below a critical tilt of 4.2° for a 1.2 mm bead, growing as 1/R². Fine beads stay where they fall; big ones run. - **Shape from the Bond number.** Below the capillary length (2.7 mm) a sphere; above it a puddle whose height saturates at 2·lc·sin(θ/2) ≈ 5.3 mm. Modelled as a superellipsoid of revolution, sphere to flat top. - **Each leaf** has a height field in its own frame: a cup deepest over the stalk, gentle hollows, the veins (found in the photograph) as faint ridges, scaled with the leaf. A stalked leaf is tipped, so its water gathers a little off-centre. The phone's tilt is turned into every leaf's frame, so one tilt rolls the beads on all of them the same way in the world. - **Quicksilver.** The film of air under the water (the plastron) mirrors the sky where the underside curves up: every bead has a silver band round its margin and lower half, the tiniest are nearly all mirror, and a pool is a flat sheet of sky with a silver rim, the window crisp near one side and the veins faint through it. A pool's outline follows the cup and keeps a lobe where a bead ran in. - **Coalescence** rings in the capillary mode (`f = √(8γ/ρR³)/2π`), shown as a few quick damped cycles slowed about four times. **Impact** (Richard, Clanet and Quéré, 2002): contact time ~2.6√(ρR³/γ), then one small rebound, stretched about three times; big drops throw off satellite droplets. - **Falling.** A bead over the edge is a free body: it keeps its speed across the pond, falls (shown at a third of g, since a real fall of 10 cm is over in a seventh of a second), shrinks with distance, and lands on the first leaf under it or in the pond, where it makes a capillary ring that spreads, slows and fades within a second. - **The pond** is still, pale, mirroring an overcast sky; higher leaves stand nearer the eye (perspective from about 62 cm) and their shadows fall on the leaves and water below, offset 0.62 mm per mm of height and softer the higher the leaf. - **Simplified:** stalks are not drawn (from above they are under the leaves); the tipped leaves are foreshortened, not modelled in 3D; a leaf's sway moves it but does not shake its beads; the pond is still except for the rings. ## How it works - **Assets.** Two Commons photographs, each cut out along its rim by tracing the edge in polar coordinates from the navel (dynamic programming over a score of the thin rim line and of leaf colour inside versus outside; the second held to an ellipse band because its neighbours are the same green). The edges are the leaves' own, sharp, 2 px anti-aliased. - **Textures.** Each image is uploaded square and mipmapped (1024²) so a small leaf never shimmers; its alpha, blurred and mipmapped (256²), is its shadow, the mip level picked from the leaf's height. - **Physics (CPU, mm and seconds),** 240 Hz substeps. Per leaf: the mask and veins of its image, its own height field (128 wide), its beads and dust. Pairs of beads that are both at rest are not tested for merging. - **Rendering (WebGL1, one context, no float textures).** 1. The pond: its outline (a soft union round the leaves and the open water between them, with a short quiet fade at the edge), the shadows of all the leaves (up to 8 casters in one pass), the rings. 2. Then each leaf from the lowest to the highest: the leaf, graded, with the shadows of the leaves above it; its beads' contact shadows and caustics (blended `dst · (src + srcα)`, so one pass darkens and brightens); its dust; its beads, ray-traced as lenses through this leaf's image, with the plastron's silver, the sky and window, and a size floor of 1.3 css px so the finest stay points of silver; the dust they carry; then any drop falling past that height. - **Loop.** Runs only while something moves (a bead rolling or in the air, a shiver, a ring, a leaf still swaying, the dimple, the colour deepening) and the pond is on screen in a visible tab. Rain waits on `setTimeout`. A slow interval watches the phone's tilt only while the pond is visible. ## Tuning Constants at the top of `lotus-leaf.js`: `PIN_ANGLE` (hysteresis), `ROLL`, `DRAG`, `TILT_DEG`, `FALL` (how slowly falls are shown), `PERSP`, `SHADOW`, `SAT0`/`SAT1`; the layouts; `rainSize()` for the mix of drop sizes. The leaf relief is in `makeLeaf()`, the pond's outline in `buildPond()`, the window and sky seen in the beads in `env()` and `sky()` in the bead shader. ## Cost - Idle it draws nothing. During the shower (about 500-600 beads on a wide layout) it holds 60 fps in desktop Chrome: one pond pass, one pass per leaf, and small quads for the beads. - DPR capped at 2. Off screen or in a hidden tab, nothing runs. If WebGL is missing or a shader fails, the ``s stay. A lost context hands back to them. ## Accessibility and reduced motion - The figure has `role="img"` and an `aria-label`; the canvas is `aria-hidden`. - Keyboard: the figure is focusable; the arrow keys tip the leaves while held, Enter or Space lets a few drops fall. - Touch: `touch-action: pan-y`, so a vertical swipe scrolls the page; a sideways push rolls a bead, press-and-hold dimples a leaf, a tap on the water makes a ring. On iOS the first tap asks for motion permission (`tilt.js`). - `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`: the finished state, computed at load (the shower settled for six seconds of simulated time): beads where they stopped, a pool in every cup, the leaves at full colour. Nothing moves. - Print shows the plain images. ## Credits - Leaves: *Nelumbo nucifera Himeji 03*, photograph by Syrio, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0; *Nelumbo nucifera feuille*, photograph by Dinkum, Wikimedia Commons, CC0. Details in `assets/credits.json`. - Physics after W. Barthlott and C. Neinhuis, "Purity of the sacred lotus, or escape from contamination in biological surfaces", *Planta* 202 (1997), and D. Richard, C. Clanet and D. Quéré, "Contact time of a bouncing drop", *Nature* 417 (2002). No third-party code. - Bud: photograph by Md. Tayhid Hasan, iNaturalist, CC BY 4.0.
